meaning: Making things that everyone can use, including people who see colors differently or need bigger text.
example: Using color-blind-safe colors and also different shapes.

meaning: Easy for everyone to use, including people who see or hear differently.
A list of exact steps, in the right order, that solves a problem or does a job.

How far you turn, measured in degrees. A full turn is 360 degrees. A shape with <math display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> sides turns <math display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>360</mn><mo>÷</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">360 \div n</annotation></semantics></math> at each corner.
example: A square turns 90 degrees at each corner.

meaning: The picture behind everything on the Scratch stage.
A Scratch message sent to every sprite. Sprites with a matching “when I receive” block start running.
A mistake in a program that makes it do something we did not want. Bugs are normal: every programmer meets them every day.
A mistake in a program / finding and fixing it.
To use a function, by writing its name with brackets.
A short check that shows what you know and what to practice next.
A color written as # and six letters or numbers, so the computer knows exactly which color you mean.
A note for humans in the code. Python ignores it. In Python it starts with #.
A question that is True or False, made with >> (bigger), << (smaller), == (equal) or != (not equal).
Code that only runs if something is true. Also called an if.

Two numbers, <math display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> and <math display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mi>y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math>, that give a place on the screen. <math display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> is left–right, <math display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mi>y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math> is down–up. The middle is <math display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mo form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(0, 0)</annotation></semantics></math>.
One of the pictures a Scratch sprite can wear. Switching costumes quickly makes animation.
Saying who made the art, sounds or ideas you used. It is fair and kind.
To find a bug and fix it. A good strategy: read the error, check the last thing you changed, test one small part at a time.
Finding and fixing bugs, step by step, like a detective.
Breaking a big problem into smaller parts that are easier to solve.
example: A house = walls + roof + door + windows.

meaning: The Python word that starts a new function (your own command).
Short for demonstration: running your program and showing how it works.
In pair programming, the person using the mouse and keyboard.
The driver clicks; the navigator reads, checks and helps.
The top part of Thonny where you write your program.
Short for “else if”: another question to check when the first if was false.
The part of an if that runs when the question is false.
The red text Python shows when it cannot run your code. It tells you the line number and a clue.
Something that happens and starts code running.
example: Clicking the green flag, pressing a key.

meaning: Extra blocks you can add to Scratch, like the Pen.
Helpful comments about someone’s work. We use “two stars and a wish”: two things you like, one idea to improve.
A card with two stars and a wish for an artist.
Python’s repeat block. The lines pushed in underneath it are repeated.
A Scratch loop that never stops (until you click the red stop sign).
A named set of steps you can use again and again. Python’s version of a My Block.
The Scratch button that starts a project.
A block or line that asks a question and only runs its steps when the answer is true.
Python’s way to choose: “if this, else if that, otherwise…”
Runs one set of blocks for yes and another for no.
Spaces at the start of a line (4 in Python). They show which lines are inside a loop, an if or a function.
Information that goes into a program, often typed by the user. In Python input() asks a question and gives back the answer as text.
A whole number, like 3, 0 or −7-7. int() turns text like "5" into the number 5.
To improve something by going round the build–run–check loop again and again.
Code that repeats. Loops save you writing the same steps again and again.
A checkpoint on the way to finishing a project.
A block you make yourself in Scratch with “Make a Block”. It can have inputs.
In pair programming, the person who reads the instructions, thinks ahead and spots bugs.
A loop inside another loop.
When a loop runs one time too many or one time too few.
What a program shows or does: text, a drawing, a sound.
Two people coding together on one computer: a driver and a navigator who swap roles.
An input that a My Block or function needs. It makes the block flexible.
Lets a sprite or turtle draw a line where it moves. Pen up: no line. Pen down: draw.
One tiny square of color. Screens make pictures out of millions of pixels.
Letting someone try your program so you can see what works and what confuses them.
The Python command that shows text in the Shell.
Keeping personal information (real name, address, school, photos, passwords) safe. We use nicknames.
A set of instructions a computer follows.
A programming language where you type words instead of dragging blocks.
Picked by chance, so you cannot guess it. Great for surprises and games.
Tells a for loop how many times to repeat.
Thinking back about what you did, what you learned and what you want next.
Making something new from someone else’s work, and giving them credit.
A Scratch loop that runs the blocks inside a set number of times.
To start a program. In Thonny, the green Run button or .
A stack of Scratch blocks that are joined together.
Scratch blocks that check things, like “touching edge?” or “key space pressed?”.
Steps that happen one after another, in order. Order matters!
The part of Thonny at the bottom where print shows text and you type answers.
An event where you show your work to others.
A character or object in Scratch that you can program.
The area in Scratch where the sprites move and the project plays.
Text in a program, written inside quotes. input() always gives a string.
The spelling and grammar rules of a programming language.
An error because the code breaks Python’s rules, like a missing bracket or colon.
Running a program on purpose to check that it works. check_my_work.py runs tests for you.
Code made of typed words and symbols.
The app we use to write and run Python.
A Python drawing tool: an arrow you move around the screen that draws lines.
A labeled box that remembers a value, like a score or an answer. The value can change.
